newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Rapid devaluation for Afghan currency.
newsitem.headline: Rapid devaluation for Afghan currency.

text.p: Afghanistan's currency, the Afghani, has undergone a rapid devaluation in Kabul, losing more than 15 per cent of its value over the last week.

Dealers in Kabul's money market on Sunday blamed the fall on the purist Islamic Taleban's failure to gain international recognition for their administration and the lack of involvement by major world powers in solving the country's problems.
"The unwillingness of foreign countries to recognise the Taleban administration has been one of the main factors for the devaluation of the Afghani," said money trader Mohammad Karim.

He added: "This has been compounded by the lack of foreign interest by the world powers in solving the Afghan conflict. Since the first days of the Taleban in Kabul, the Afghani has fallen more than 60 per cent."

When Kabul first fell to the Taleban in late September last year, the Afghani rose by more than 50 per cent on the back of hopes for peace and stability, falling from 23,000 Afghanis to 11,000 Afghanis to the dollar. On Sunday afternoon the price was 28,200 Afghanis to the dollar.

Aid workers say the devaluation will add further misery to the city's hard pressed population. "All the food in Kabul's markets is bought with hard currency in Pakistan," said Ismael Omer, head of the United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) in Kabul.
"Poor people will never be able to afford the food," he said. "The people here are already struggling to survive. The fall in the value of the Afghani will make inflation even worse."
According to WFP statistics, the price of wheatflour, one of the basic constituents of the diet of ordinary Afghans, rose by 280 per cent during 1996.

Planes believed to belong to the anti-Taleban alliance dropped two bombs on Kabul's airport on Sunday. Witnesses said there was no damage to buildings or facilities at the airport, which is used for both military and civilian traffic.

The raid at 8.30 a.m. (0400 GMT) provoked prolonged bursts of anti-aircraft fire from Taleban gunners. At least one ground-to-air missile was also fired but it did not appear to hit the attacking plane.

There have been a number of air raids aimed at the airport since the Taleban took Kabul, but they have so far failed to put it out of commission. One raid on January 5 hit a suburb near the airport, killing four people and wounding 15.
